usage: Refers specifically to the big lunar holidays 설날 and 추석, not just any day off.
The standard greeting you say to coworkers and neighbors before the break.
명절 plus 연휴; the multi-day stretch most people get off work.
Set phrase used on the news for 설날 and 추석.
examples: 이번 명절에는 고향에 내려가요?
Are you going to your hometown this holiday?
내려가다 = to go down (to one's hometown); a classic holiday small-talk question.
명절만 되면 차가 너무 막혀요.
Whenever a holiday comes around the traffic is terrible.
-만 되면 = every time it becomes; refers to the famous holiday gridlock.
저는 명절에 일하는 대신 평일에 쉬어요.
Instead of working on holidays I take weekdays off.
-는 대신 = instead of; common for service-industry workers.
nuance: 명절 is the word for Korea's two major lunar-calendar holidays, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (the harvest festival), when the whole country travels home to family. It carries a strong sense of family duty and reunion, so asking about someone's 명절 plans is a normal, slightly personal greeting. Smaller red-letter days like Children's Day are 공휴일, not 명절.
mistakes: Don't use 명절 for every public holiday; a single day off like 광복절 is a 공휴일, while 명절 means the big lunar reunions.
Saying 명절 축하해요 sounds off — Koreans say 명절 잘 보내세요 (spend the holiday well), not 'congratulations'.

usage: A softer, native-Korean name for 추석; common in greetings and on cards.
The set holiday greeting you'll get by text from companies and friends.
may it always be as good as Chuseok
From the proverb 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라.
풍성하다 = plentiful; a fixed warm phrase for the harvest holiday.
examples: 행복한 한가위 보내세요!
Have a happy Chuseok!
The most common holiday-greeting text you'll send and receive.
한가위에는 보름달을 보면서 소원을 빌어요.
On Chuseok people make a wish while looking at the full moon.
보름달 = full moon; 소원을 빌다 = to make a wish.
한가위는 추석을 부르는 예쁜 우리말이에요.
Hangawi is the pretty native-Korean name for Chuseok.
Explains the relationship between the two words to a learner.
nuance: 한가위 is the warm, native-Korean name for 추석, the autumn harvest festival held on the 15th of the eighth lunar month. You'll see it most in greetings and holiday cards, where 행복한 한가위 보내세요 sounds friendlier than the plain 추석. The famous saying 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라 expresses a wish that life were always as bountiful as this season.
mistakes: 한가위 and 추석 mean the same holiday; 한가위 is just the softer native name, so don't treat them as two separate days.
It's spelled 한가위 (ending in 위), not 한가의 — the last syllable is 위, not 의.

usage: Several days off in a row; the thing everyone plans trips around.
황금 = golden; an extra-long break when holidays line up with the weekend.
계획 = plan; a standard topic of conversation before the break.
When a workday falls between two days off, often taken as leave to bridge them.
examples: 이번 추석은 연휴가 길어서 좋아요.
This Chuseok the long weekend is nice and long.
-아서 좋다 = good because; people love when 연휴 stretches out.
연휴라 비행기표가 다 매진됐어요.
Because it's a long weekend the plane tickets are all sold out.
매진되다 = to sell out; demand spikes during 연휴.
연휴 잘 보내고 오세요.
Enjoy the long weekend (and come back well).
A natural send-off to coworkers before the break.
nuance: 연휴 means a run of consecutive days off, the practical thing Koreans actually plan around rather than a single holiday. When a 명절 or public holiday connects with a weekend it becomes a 황금연휴 (golden long weekend), and people often burn a vacation day on a 징검다리 (stepping-stone) workday to extend it. Flights and trains sell out fast, so locals book early.
mistakes: 연휴 specifically means several days off in a row; for one single day off use 휴일, not 연휴.
Don't confuse 연휴 (consecutive days off) with 휴가 (your personal vacation/leave) — a 연휴 is on the calendar for everyone.

usage: The morning ceremony for ancestors held on 설날 and 추석.
지내다 is the set verb for holding the ceremony.
The table of food arranged for the 차례.
The dishes prepared specifically for the ceremony.
examples: 설날 아침에 차례를 지내고 떡국을 먹어요.
On Seollal morning we hold the ancestral rite and then eat tteokguk.
The standard order of a Lunar New Year morning.
요즘은 차례를 간소하게 지내는 집도 많아요.
These days many households hold the rite in a simplified way.
간소하게 = simply; reflects a real modern trend.
저희 집은 차례를 안 지내고 여행을 가요.
Our family doesn't do the rite and goes traveling instead.
Increasingly common, especially among younger families.
nuance: 차례 is the simplified ancestral memorial rite performed on the morning of 설날 and 추석, where families set out food and bow to honor their ancestors. It differs from 제사, the rite held on the anniversary of a specific person's death. Many younger households now hold 차례 in a pared-down form or skip it to travel, which is increasingly accepted.
mistakes: 차례 (holiday rite) and 제사 (death-anniversary rite) are not the same; use 제사 for the yearly memorial of a specific ancestor.
The verb is 차례를 지내다 (hold the rite), not 차례를 하다 — 지내다 is the fixed pairing.

english: New Year's deep bow to elders
usage: The formal deep bow children and juniors make on 설날.
to make the New Year's bow
하다 verb; what you do to grandparents and parents on Seollal.
Cash elders give after receiving a 세배; read '세배똔'.
Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)
The phrase you say while doing the 세배.
examples: 설날에 할머니께 세배를 했어요.
On Seollal I bowed to my grandmother.
께 is the honorific 'to'; bowing to elders is the core ritual.
세배하면 어른들이 세뱃돈을 주세요.
When you do the New Year's bow, the elders give you money.
The cause-and-effect kids look forward to most.
세배할 때 '새해 복 많이 받으세요'라고 말해요.
While bowing you say 'Happy New Year.'
-라고 말하다 = to say (quoted); the standard accompanying line.
nuance: 세배 is the deep, formal bow that younger people give to elders on 설날 to wish them a good year, said together with 새해 복 많이 받으세요. In return, elders offer words of advice and 세뱃돈 (New Year's cash), which children eagerly collect. Even as adults, you'll likely perform 세배 to parents and grandparents at the holiday gathering.
mistakes: Don't mix up 세배 (the bow) with 세뱃돈 (the money received afterward) — they're related but different words.
세배 is the proper deep bow to elders, not a casual nod; performing it carelessly can read as disrespectful.

usage: Kind, encouraging wishes elders give, especially at New Year.
하다 verb; what an elder does after receiving your 세배.
나누다 = to share; people trade 덕담 at the holiday table.
한마디 = a word/remark; 'say a few kind words' on a happy occasion.
examples: 세배를 하면 어른들이 덕담을 해 주세요.
After you bow, the elders offer words of blessing.
해 주다 = to do (for someone); the elder's part of the 세배 exchange.
새해에는 건강하라는 덕담을 많이 들었어요.
For the new year I heard lots of wishes to stay healthy.
-라는 = quoted wish ('be healthy'); typical New Year 덕담.
결혼식에서 어른이 덕담 한마디 해 주셨어요.
At the wedding an elder said a few words of blessing.
덕담 isn't only for New Year; it fits any happy occasion.
nuance: 덕담 means the warm, encouraging words of blessing that elders give younger people, most famously right after receiving a 세배 on 설날. The wishes are usually about health, success, or marriage, and accepting them gracefully is part of the ritual. Beyond New Year, 덕담 also covers the kind remarks an elder offers at weddings and other celebrations.
mistakes: 덕담 is specifically positive, blessing-type talk for happy occasions — it's never used for advice that scolds or criticizes.
The verb is 덕담을 하다/나누다, not 덕담을 말하다; pair it with 하다 or 나누다 to sound natural.

english: rice-cake soup eaten on New Year
usage: Sliced rice cakes in broth; the must-eat dish on 설날 morning.
Eating a bowl on New Year symbolically adds a year to your age.
그릇 = bowl; the counter and the joking unit of 'aging' one year.
A popular variant with 만두 (dumplings) added.
examples: 설날 아침에는 떡국을 꼭 먹어요.
On Seollal morning we always eat tteokguk.
꼭 = without fail; the defining New Year food custom.
떡국 한 그릇 먹으면 한 살 더 먹는 거예요.
Eating a bowl of tteokguk means you turn a year older.
한 살 더 먹다 = to age one year; a beloved New Year joke.
저는 떡국보다 떡만둣국을 더 좋아해요.
I like rice-cake-and-dumpling soup more than plain tteokguk.
-보다 더 = more than; comparing the two versions.
nuance: 떡국 is the soup of thinly sliced rice cakes in clear broth that Koreans eat on the morning of 설날. There's a long-running joke that finishing a bowl means you've officially gained a year, so people ask 떡국 몇 그릇 먹었어? to tease about age. A common, heartier variant is 떡만둣국, which adds dumplings to the same broth.
mistakes: Don't confuse 떡국 (savory rice-cake soup) with 떡볶이 (spicy stir-fried rice cakes) — different dishes despite both using 떡.
The New Year 'aging' line is a joke about 떡국; eating it doesn't really change your legal age, especially since the age-counting law changed.

usage: Stuffed, pine-steamed rice cakes; the signature 추석 food.
빚다 is the special verb for forming dough by hand.
A common filling; others include 콩 (beans) and 밤 (chestnut).
송편 is steamed over 솔잎, which gives it its scent.
examples: 추석에는 온 가족이 모여서 송편을 빚어요.
On Chuseok the whole family gathers to make songpyeon.
온 가족 = the whole family; making them together is the tradition.
송편을 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는대요.
They say if you shape songpyeon prettily you'll have a pretty daughter.
-는대요 = they say; a well-known playful old saying.
저는 깨송편이 제일 맛있어요.
Sesame songpyeon is the tastiest to me.
제일 = most; naming a favorite filling.
nuance: 송편 are small half-moon-shaped rice cakes stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut and steamed over pine needles, eaten at 추석. Families traditionally gather to shape them by hand using the verb 빚다, and there's a charming saying that making them neatly foretells a pretty daughter. The pine-needle steaming gives them their distinctive 솔잎 fragrance.
mistakes: 송편 pairs with the verb 빚다 (to shape by hand), not 만들다 in the traditional phrasing — 송편을 빚다 sounds most natural.
송편 is the 추석 rice cake; don't confuse it with 떡국's rice cakes or generic 떡 — it's a specific shaped, filled variety.

usage: Visiting ancestors' graves to pay respects, especially at 추석.
가다 verb; the family outing to the gravesite during the holiday.
Cutting the overgrown grass on the mound, often done before 추석.
산소 = the burial mound you visit during 성묘.
examples: 추석에 가족들이랑 성묘를 다녀왔어요.
I went to visit the family graves with relatives for Chuseok.
다녀오다 = to go and come back; the typical holiday grave visit.
성묘 가기 전에 벌초부터 했어요.
Before the grave visit we first cleared the grass.
-부터 = first of all; 벌초 usually precedes 성묘.
요즘은 성묘 대신 납골당에 가는 사람도 많아요.
These days many people go to a charnel house instead of tending graves.
납골당 = columbarium; reflects changing burial customs.
nuance: 성묘 is the custom of visiting ancestors' graves to clean them and bow in respect, done above all at 추석 and 설날. It often follows 벌초, the chore of cutting back the grass on the 산소 (burial mound). As cremation has become the norm, more families now visit a 납골당 (columbarium) instead, but the word 성묘 still covers paying these respects.
mistakes: 성묘 is going to the grave; 차례 is the food-table rite at home — they're separate parts of the holiday, not synonyms.
Don't confuse 성묘 (visiting/tending graves) with 벌초 (the specific task of cutting the grass) — 벌초 is one step within a 성묘 trip.

english: the 15th of the lunar month; full-moon day
usage: The midpoint of a lunar month, when the moon is full.
the first full moon of the year
A traditional holiday on the 15th of the first lunar month.
달 = moon; the round moon seen on a 보름 night.
보름 also colloquially means a span of about 15 days.
examples: 정월대보름에는 부럼을 깨 먹어요.
On the first full moon we crack and eat nuts (burum).
부럼 = nuts cracked for health; a 대보름 custom.
오늘 밤 보름달이 정말 크고 밝아요.
Tonight's full moon is really big and bright.
보름달 = full moon; a natural everyday remark.
여행 간 지 벌써 보름이 지났어요.
It's already been about half a month since the trip.
보름 here means roughly 15 days, a common colloquial use.
nuance: 보름 literally marks the 15th day of the lunar month, the night of the full moon, and by extension is used casually to mean a span of about half a month. The big related holiday is 정월대보름, the first full moon of the year, when people crack 부럼 nuts and eat 오곡밥 for health and luck. In daily speech you'll most often hear it as 보름달 (full moon).
mistakes: 보름 by itself is the 15th / full-moon day; the actual holiday is 정월대보름, so don't shorten the holiday's name to just 보름.
When 보름 means a duration it's roughly 15 days — don't read it as exactly two weeks (14 days).

english: the dog days of summer (hottest days)
usage: The three hottest marked days of summer: 초복, 중복, 말복.
삼복 = the three bok days; the fiercest stretch of summer heat.
eat samgyetang on a bok day
The custom of eating hot ginseng-chicken soup to beat the heat.
The three 복날 spread across mid-to-late summer.
examples: 복날이라 삼계탕집 앞에 줄이 길어요.
It's a bok day so the line in front of the samgyetang place is long.
Eating 삼계탕 on 복날 causes famous lunchtime queues.
오늘이 초복인데 보양식 먹으러 갈까요?
Today's the first bok day — shall we go eat some restorative food?
보양식 = stamina/restorative food; -ㄹ까요 invites.
삼복더위에는 밖에 나가기도 싫어요.
During the peak-bok heat I don't even want to go outside.
-기도 싫다 = don't even want to; describes the brutal heat.
nuance: 복날 refers to the three hottest days of summer in the lunar calendar — 초복, 중복, and 말복 — collectively the time of 삼복더위, the fiercest heat. The custom is to eat a hot, restorative 보양식 like 삼계탕 to fight heat with heat, so famous soup restaurants get long lunchtime lines on these days. The dates appear on most Korean calendars.
mistakes: 복날 isn't one fixed day; it's three separate days (초복, 중복, 말복) spread through summer, so use them by name when you mean a specific one.
Despite the heat, the 복날 custom is hot soup, not cold food — saying you'll eat 냉면 to 'celebrate' 복날 misses the point.

usage: Worn on 명절, at weddings, and now for fun photos at palaces.
입다 = to wear; the verb for putting on the outfit.
대여 = rental; you rent 한복 to enter palaces free in Seoul.
A modernized, casual version designed for daily wear.
examples: 설날에 한복을 입고 세배를 했어요.
On Seollal I wore hanbok and did the New Year's bow.
Wearing 한복 for the 명절 rite is the classic occasion.
경복궁은 한복을 입으면 입장료가 무료예요.
Gyeongbokgung is free admission if you wear hanbok.
무료 = free; a popular reason young people rent 한복.
요즘은 생활한복을 평소에 입는 사람도 있어요.
These days some people wear modern hanbok in daily life.
평소에 = normally; reflects the 생활한복 trend.
nuance: 한복 is traditional Korean clothing, worn most often on 명절, at weddings, and at first-birthday parties, with the verb 입다. For young people and visitors it's also a popular activity to rent 한복 near palaces like Gyeongbokgung, since wearing it gets you free admission and great photos. A modernized 생활한복 is increasingly seen as everyday wear.
mistakes: 한복 takes 입다 (to wear/put on like clothes), not 쓰다 or 신다 — those are for hats and shoes respectively.
한복 isn't only a museum costume; treating it as purely old-fashioned ignores the trendy rental and 생활한복 culture among 20-30s.
